name: Rhabdomyolysis

matching.reasoningTemplate: Muscle pain with tea-coloured urine and very high CK indicates rhabdomyolysis with AKI risk.

redFlags: Aggressive fluids; watch hyperkalaemia and AKI

clinicalPearls: Myoglobinuria characteristically produces a positive urine dipstick for blood while urine microscopy shows no (or few) red cells — a key clue distinguishing pigment nephropathy from true haematuria (Harrison 22e p.343).

In rhabdomyolysis-associated acute tubular necrosis the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) may be paradoxically low (<1%), unlike the classic >1% of established ATN, because the injury is often early/non-oliguric (Harrison 22e p.343).
Rhabdomyolysis is listed among the 'don't-miss' metabolic emergencies whose urgency can be underappreciated, alongside malignant hyperthermia and tumour lysis syndrome (Harrison 22e p.102).

Heat-related exertional rhabdomyolysis is a recognised, albeit rare, cause of sudden death in sickle cell trait carriers during strenuous exercise — a reason to counsel carriers before sports participation (Harrison 22e p.818).
harrison.pathophysiology: Massive skeletal muscle breakdown releases intracellular contents — including myoglobin, potassium, phosphate and creatine kinase — into the circulation. Filtered myoglobin (a heme protein) is nephrotoxic and contributes to pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis; the released heme pigment also causes a false-positive dipstick reaction for blood. Concurrent volume sequestration into injured muscle produces a prerenal/hypovolaemic insult that compounds the tubular injury (Harrison 22e p.343).
infectionMimics: Clostridial myositis/myonecrosis — predictably precipitates acute rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096).
Streptococcal (group A) myositis — also predictably causes acute rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096).
Viral myositis — influenza, echovirus, coxsackievirus and Epstein-Barr virus infections may be associated with rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096).
Legionella infection — reported association with rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096).
additionalInvestigations: Urine dipstick for blood with microscopy — dipstick blood-positive but RBC-negative supports myoglobinuria rather than true haematuria (Harrison 22e p.343).
Urine sediment / microscopy for muddy-brown (pigmented) granular casts and tubular epithelial cells, indicating accompanying acute tubular necrosis (Harrison 22e p.343).
Serum phosphate and calcium — hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia accompany acute muscle injury (Harrison 22e p.359, p.363).
Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) — may be <1% in early rhabdomyolysis-associated ATN, limiting its discriminatory value (Harrison 22e p.343).
redFlags: Hyperkalaemia from release of intracellular potassium during muscle necrosis — predictable and potentially life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.359).
Rising creatinine with pigmented granular casts signalling evolving pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis (Harrison 22e p.343).
harrison.prognosis: Rhabdomyolysis-associated acute kidney injury is frequently of the milder, non-oliguric ATN type and is potentially reversible with adequate perfusion; the recovery phase may be complicated by rebound hypercalcaemia (Harrison 22e p.343, p.362).
pitfalls: Interpreting a dipstick-positive 'haematuria' as bleeding from the urinary tract when no RBCs are seen on microscopy — this pattern reflects myoglobinuria in rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.343).
Relying on a low FENa to exclude ATN: rhabdomyolysis-related ATN can present with FENa <1% (Harrison 22e p.343).

Acute rhabdomyolysis typically causes hypocalcaemia, but the recovery phase (with renal failure) can produce rebound hypercalcaemia — calcium should not be over-corrected early (Harrison 22e p.362, p.363).

valueTables.title: Drug-induced myopathies and their toxic reactions

rows.parameter: Lipid-lowering agents (fibrates, HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, niacin)

cells.text: All three classes can cause a range of toxicity: raised serum creatine kinase without symptoms, myalgias, exercise-induced pain, rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria
Acute high-dose treatment can cause acute quadriplegic myopathy, often together with nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers but also without them; chronic use mainly causes proximal weakness
Acute quadriplegic myopathy, with or without glucocorticoids
Mitochondrial myopathy with ragged red fibers

rows.parameter: Drugs of abuse (alcohol, amphetamines, cocaine, heroin, phencyclidine, meperidine)

cells.text: Widespread muscle breakdown, rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria; local injection causes muscle necrosis, skin induration and limb contractures
May cause polymyositis and myasthenia gravis
Painless proximal weakness with autophagic vacuoles on muscle biopsy
Painless proximal weakness, especially in renal failure; biopsy shows autophagic vacuoles
cimetidine, cocaine, cyclosporine, danazol, emetine, gold, heroin, labetalol, methadone, d-penicillamine, statins and other cholesterol-lowering agents, l-tryptophan, zidovudine
